column4: ### The Body
column5: ### Body

column4: The church is often described as **the Body of Christ**, emphasizing both its unity and diversity. With Christ as the head, the church functions as a living organism where every believer plays an essential and potentially diverse role. Each member is uniquely gifted and contributes to the health and mission of the body according to their own function. This image highlights the interdependence of believers, specifically that the body must be connected to function, and that our function is collaborative not competitive. When every part works together, the body grows and thrives in unity and love (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18).

With Christ as the head, the church functions like a living organism, where every believer plays an essential and often different role. Each member is endowed with unique gifts and contributes to the health and mission of the body according to their particular function. This image illuminates the interdependence of believers, specifically that for the body to function it must be connected, and that our work is collaborative, not competitive. When each part works together, the body grows and flourishes in unity and love (1 Corinthians 12:12-27; Ephesians 4:15-16; Colossians 1:18).

column4: ### The Bride
column5: ### Bride

column4: The church is described as **the Bride of Christ**, this reflects an intimate and loving relationship with Jesus. Just as a bride is cherished and made ready for her husband, the church is sanctified and purified by Christ’s sacrificial love. This metaphor captures the devotion and faithfulness expected of the church, as well as the deep affection Christ has for His people. The imagery also points to the ultimate union between Christ and the church, celebrated in the marriage supper of the Lamb, where the church is presented in glory without spot or blemish (Ephesians 5:25-27; Revelation 19:7-9; Revelation 21:2).

column4: ### The Temple
column5: ### Temple

column4: The church is described as **the Temple of God**, the dwelling place of His Spirit. Believers are described as living stones being built together on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Himself as the cornerstone. This holy structure signifies God’s presence among His people and their role as a community of worship and prayer. The temple imagery underscores the importance of holiness and the church’s collective purpose in glorifying God (1 Corinthians 3:16-17; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-5).

column4: ### The Family
column5: ### Family

column4: The church is described as **the Family of God**, emphasizing relational unity and care among its members. Through the Spirit of adoption, believers are made children of God and members of His household. This familial imagery highlights the love, belonging, and shared inheritance believers have in Christ. It also reflects the call to treat one another with compassion and humility as brothers and sisters in God’s family (Galatians 6:10; Ephesians 2:19; Romans 8:15-17). Furthermore, through the family image it depicts how the members of the church are to become mature, that they would be taught and nourished by spiritual mothers and fathers (1 Timothy 5:1-2), that we could go from infants drinking the pure milk of the Word, to full grown adults able to eat the strong meat of the Word (Hebrews 5).

column4: ### The Flock
column5: ### Flock

column4: The church is described as **the Flock**, sheep under the care of Jesus, the Good Shepherd. This image conveys the church’s dependence on Christ for guidance, sustenance, and protection. It also emphasizes the responsibility of church leaders to faithfully shepherd God’s flock as under shepherds, mirroring Christ’s example of love and care. The flock imagery speaks to trust, obedience, and the close relationship between the Great Shepherd and His sheep (John 10:14-16; 1 Peter 5:2; Acts 20:28).

column4: ### The Vine and Branches
column5: ### Vine and Branches

column4: The church is described as **the Vine and Branches**, illustrating the essential connection between believers and Christ. Jesus is the true vine, and believers are the branches that must remain in Him to bear fruit. This metaphor highlights dependence on Christ for spiritual vitality, growth, and productivity. Without Him, believers can do nothing, but by abiding in Him, they glorify God and fulfill their purpose. Jesus will prune so that He can bear more fruit in our lives (John 15:1-5).

Apart from him, believers can do nothing, but by remaining in him they glorify God and fulfill their purpose. Jesus will prune so that he may bring forth more fruit in our lives (John 15:1-5).

column4: The church’s mission, like the Holy Spirit's role, can be understood through three dimensions: upward, inward, and outward, each reflecting a unique aspect of its calling in God’s plan. These dimensions guide the church in fulfilling its role as a worshiping, edifying, and missional community.

column4: ### Upward: Worship and Glorifying God
column5: ### Upward: Worship and Glorifying God

column4: The church’s first purpose is to worship and glorify God. Corporate worship, where believers gather to exalt God together, is a visible reflection of His glory and a response to His greatness. As the psalmist declares, “*Worship the Lord in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth*” (Psalms 96:9). Beyond corporate worship, the church is called to live lives of obedience and sacrifice, offering themselves as “living sacrifices” as an act of spiritual worship (Romans 12:1-2). This upward focus keeps the church centered on God’s majesty and aligns its priorities with His will.

column4: The church at Jerusalem was led primarily by the **apostles**, who focused on teaching, prayer, and spiritual oversight (Acts 2:42, Acts 6:4). As the community grew, the need for administrative structure became apparent, particularly to address practical matters like caring for widows and distributing resources. This led to the appointment of **deacons** (Acts 6:1-7). These individuals, chosen for their spiritual maturity and good reputation, handled practical ministries to allow the apostles to focus on their spiritual responsibilities. Over time, **elders** also emerged as leaders in the Jerusalem church. For instance, during the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), both apostles and elders were involved in decision-making, showing a collaborative leadership structure.
column5: The church in Jerusalem was led primarily by the apostles, who focused on teaching, prayer, and spiritual care (Acts 2:42, Acts 6:4)। As the community grew, the need for administrative structure became clear, especially to address practical issues such as the care of widows and the distribution of resources। This led to the appointment of **deacons** (Acts 6:1-7)। Chosen on the basis of spiritual maturity and good reputation, these individuals handled practical ministries so that the apostles could concentrate on their spiritual responsibilities। Over time, **elders** also emerged as leaders in the church in Jerusalem। For example, during the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15), both the apostles and the elders participated in decision-making, indicating a shared leadership structure।

column4: ### Church at Antioch
column5: ### The church in Antioch

column4: The church at Antioch had a more decentralized and diverse leadership structure compared to Jerusalem. It was led by a group of **prophets and teachers**, including Barnabas, Saul (Paul), Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen (Acts 13:1). The church at Antioch was also much more oriented towards reaching the gentiles, where the church in Jerusalem reflected more of its Jewish roots. While the New Testament does not explicitly mention deacons in Antioch, it is likely that practical roles existed given the church's growing size and involvement in sending relief to Jerusalem (Acts 11:29-30). The church at Antioch became a model for commissioning missionaries, with leaders praying, fasting, and laying hands on Paul and Barnabas to send them out (Acts 13:2-3). This demonstrates a structure that balanced spiritual oversight (prophets and teachers) with missional outreach and practical support.
column5: The leadership of the church in Antioch was more decentralized and diverse than that of Jerusalem। It was led by a group of **prophets and teachers**, including Barnabas, Saul (Paul), Simeon, Lucius, and Manaen (Acts 13:1)। The church in Antioch was also much more focused on reaching Gentiles, whereas the church in Jerusalem reflected its Jewish roots more strongly। Although the New Testament does not explicitly mention deacons in Antioch, given the growing size of the church and its participation in sending relief to Jerusalem, it is likely that practical roles existed (Acts 11:29-30)। The church in Antioch became a model for the appointment of missionaries, where the leaders prayed, fasted, and laid hands on Paul and Barnabas to send them out (Acts 13:2-3)। This illustrates a structure that balances spiritual care (prophets and teachers) with missional outreach and practical support।

column4: Unlike Paul’s corrections to the Corinthians and Galatians, the scriptures do not critique the leadership structures of Jerusalem or Antioch. This suggests that these churches, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, were free to adapt their gatherings to meet their unique needs and circumstances within the framework of sound doctrine and apostolic teaching (Acts 2:42, 2 Timothy 3:16-17).

column4: So far in this chapter we’ve covered the leadership of the church and the core analogies for the church. Let’s build upon the specific analogy of *the body* and consider a marathon runner.

column4: ### You Are a Part of the Whole
column5: ### You are part of the whole

column4: The church, as the Body of Christ, depends on every member working together to fulfill its mission. Just as the body cannot function properly if one part is missing, the church needs each believer to actively participate, grow, and serve. Each member of the body has a very important role. To be part of the body means staying connected. A body can survive at diminished capacity without a limb, but the limb itself cannot live when separated from the body. We must be an active part of the church and not become dismembered. Hebrews 10:24 says that we should gather and not forsake the assembly.

To be part of the body is to remain connected. A body can live with reduced capacity without a limb, but that limb cannot live separated from the body. We must remain active parts of the Church and not become detached. Hebrews 10:24 says that we should meet together and not forsake the assembly.

column4: To really work and function together you need to fellowship! You need to know others, love others and ideally like others! Build strong relationships and friendships and repair them when they become stressed or injured. When a joint gets injured or inflamed, you need to work to rest and or reset it; so that the joint that’s dislodged doesn’t become broken! A broken and unhealing limb will eventually be separated, and you cannot be part of the body, alone.

column4: Believers must train and equip for their unique roles in the church, just as a runner strengthens specific muscles for the race. You won’t be successful if you jump into a marathon and haven’t trained, and not all training is equal, you need to be adequately prepared for the race. Jesus has given specific ministry gifts to equip believers, not to do all the work themselves, but to empower every member to serve effectively in their unique roles.

Jesus gave specific ministry gifts to equip believers, so that they would not do all the work themselves, but would empower every member to serve effectively in their unique role.

This does not imply blind obedience or control but reflects a spirit of reverence and cooperation. Worldly submission is demanded by those in authority and can be degrading and lead to resentment. column4: Practice giving. We can give to the church in many important ways, and we are instructed to do so to accomplish the mission.
column5: Practice giving. We can give to the church in many meaningful ways, and we are instructed to do so to accomplish the mission.

column4: - Time - we can give our time and volunteer. When we give our time, we use our efforts and our talents. This can also be a great way to learn new skills and increase existing ones.
column5: - Time - We can give our time and volunteer. When we give our time, we apply our effort and use our gifts. This can also be a great way to learn new skills and sharpen existing ones.

column4: - Resources - we can give of our resources. Most commonly today this is probably giving financially to the church and to ministries (not just the “institution”, but those in need in the church). Giving money is useful, because the church can buy needed resources with it, but people have given their physical resources beyond money, for example extra homes, clothing, cars, food, building materials, tools, etc. In Acts 4:32-35 we see an example of early believers giving freely, sharing proceeds from sale of extra lands and homes and giving so that ‘none had need’.
column5: - Resources - We can give our resources. Most commonly today this means giving financially to the church and ministries (not only to the “organization,” but also to those in need within the church). Giving money is useful, since the church can purchase needed resources with it, but people have also given their material resources beyond money, for example extra houses, clothing, cars, food, building materials, tools, etc. In Acts 4:32-35 we see the example of the early believers who gave generously, sharing the proceeds from the sale of extra lands and houses, and giving in such a way that ‘no one was in need’.

column4: Working alongside others in ministry can reveal your strengths and deepen your understanding of your role. Engage in small groups or church activities to foster connections. Listen to the burdens and needs of those around you and consider how you can support them. Building relationships within the church helps you connect with others and understand the community’s needs.
column5: Serving alongside others can reveal your strengths and deepen your understanding of your role. Attend small groups or church activities to increase connection. Listen to the burdens and needs of those around you and consider how you can support them. Building relationships within the church helps you connect with others and understand the needs of the community.

column4: #### Step 4 - Get Help!
column5: #### Step 4 - Get help!

column4: Jesus said that in life we would experience trouble! (John 16:33) We are encouraged to not carry the weight of our burdens by ourselves but to cast them on God who cares for us! (1 Peter 5:7)
column5: Jesus said that in life we will have troubles! (John 16:33) We are encouraged not to carry our burdens ourselves, but to cast them upon God, who cares for us! (1 Peter 5:7)

column4: Sometimes in our journey we may become injured. Marathon runners, even when doing “everything right” can stress their bodies to the point of injury, or they can trip and fall.
column5: Sometimes on our journey we may become injured. Marathon runners, even while doing “everything right,” can stress their bodies to the point of injury, or they may stumble and fall.

column4: Not all ‘falling’ is sin related, but some of it is, not all weakness is ‘our fault’, sometimes others will sin against us. Regardless for the cause of our weakness or injury we are to be restored and healed.
column5: Not every ‘fall’ is related to sin, though some are; not every weakness is ‘our fault’; sometimes others even sin against us. Whatever the cause of our weakness or injury, we are to be restored and healed.

column4: There is great freedom in seeking inner healing and restoration. We are called to cover the vulnerable parts of the body (1 Corinthians 12:23) and to restore those caught in trespasses (Galatians 6:1).
column5: There is great freedom in seeking inner healing and restoration. We are called to cover the more modest parts of the body (1 Corinthians 12:23) and to restore those who are caught in trespasses (Galatians 6:1).

column4: There is much to say about this topic, and we explore the themes of healing as an overview in the chapter on sanctification.
column5: There is much to say on this topic, and we briefly explore themes of healing in the chapter on sanctification.

column4: #### Step 5 - Be Patient
column5: #### Step 5 - Persevere

column4: Pay attention to confirmation from God and others. Often, God confirms your calling through fruitfulness, joy, and affirmation from those around you. Reflect on where your efforts have borne fruit and listen to feedback about the impact of the ministry. This can help you recognize where you are most effective in serving the Body of Christ.
column5: Pay attention to confirmation that comes from God and others. Often, God confirms your calling through fruitfulness, joy, and the affirmation of those around you. Consider where your efforts have borne fruit and listen to feedback about the impact of your service. This can help you discern where you are most effective in serving the Body of Christ.

column4: Be patient and trust God’s timing. Discovering your role may take time and involve trial and error (Philippians 1:6). Trust that God will guide you as you remain faithful and open to His leading. During this time, commit to growth and training by attending workshops, Bible studies, and other resources that equip you for service. Do this with the church, engage with the body of Christ to discover your gifting.
column5: Be patient and trust God’s timing. It may take time to discover your role and may involve trial and error (Philippians 1:6). Trust that as you remain faithful and open to His guidance, God will guide you. In the meantime, stay committed to growth and preparation by engaging in workshops, Bible studies, and other resources that equip you for ministry. Do this together with the church; stay connected to the Body of Christ as you discover your spiritual gifts.

column4: Remember, the church is not a building or an institution; it is a living, breathing body made up of people like you. By stepping into your role, you contribute to its mission and glorify Christ as its head.
column5: Remember, the church is not a building or an institution; it is a living, breathing body made up of people like you. By stepping into your role, you contribute to its mission and give glory to Christ, who is its head.
